title: Locks: row, table and advisory, and what blocks what

videos.script: Somebody adds a column to a table. The statement takes two milliseconds. {{alter}} For the next fifteen seconds, every query on that table stops. Even the cheapest read of one row waits. {{stall}} Nothing was broken. Two correct statements met in the wrong order. {{order}} This lesson is about those meetings. You open two or three terminals on the same database, and you make them wait for each other on purpose. {{windows}} First the table locks that every statement takes, even a plain select, and the matrix of which ones conflict. {{matrix}} Then row locks: two writers on one row, a lock that refuses instead of waiting, and a job queue that skips what is taken. {{rows}} Then the queue itself, where a waiting statement makes everybody behind it wait too, and the setting that stops it. {{queue}} Then advisory locks, for a job only one worker should run. {{advisory}} And last, a real deadlock: two transactions each waiting for the other, the error the server raises, and the habit that makes it impossible. {{deadlock}} By the end, a query that is suddenly slow for no reason of its own will make you ask one question first. What is it waiting for? {{title}}
